tagline: Mountain gaps and waterfalls frame a loop through the Chattahoochee headwaters.
intro: The Russell–Brasstown byway winds through southern Appalachian valleys and mountain gaps within the Chattahoochee National Forest. Its loop encircles the Chattahoochee River headwaters; the Forest Service gives the drive as 40 miles and recommends at least three hours. A National Scenic Byway since June 15, 2000, it includes Georgia’s highest mountain, Brasstown Bald. The Forest Service highlights wildflowers, fall color and views into wilderness valleys.

The loop came together through improvements to several numbered roads. Its SR 75 section was established in 1932 and paved by the end of 1946. In 1966, two parts of SR 348 were joined, completing a paved circuit. National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1989. Before that final connection, the SR 75 section had progressed from graded earth to a semi-hard surface by July 1939. Paving and the joining of SR 348 preceded the later scenic designations: the touring route inherited roads built in stages.

For a circuit beginning at Brasstown Bald, descend the spur to SR 180 and take the eastern side toward SR 17/75. Head south toward Helen, then use SR 75 Alternate to reach SR 348. Follow SR 348 northwest to Choestoe and SR 180 back toward the summit spur.

moments.title: Brasstown Bald
moments.text: Brasstown Bald is Georgia’s highest point, known to the Cherokee people as Enotah. The Forest Service describes a summit view spanning 360 degrees of rolling highlands. The mountain also carries a monument to someone who worked to bring visitors here: former Georgia Supreme Court Judge Thomas S. Candler. Erected in 1971, three months before his death, the stone recognizes his support for attracting visitors and establishing a visitor center. On a clear day, the tallest buildings in Atlanta can be seen from the summit, some 85 miles away.

moments.title: Dukes Creek Falls
moments.text: Dukes Creek Falls carries one creek’s name but drops on another: Davis Creek, at its meeting with Dukes Creek. An observation platform faces the falls. The Forest Service describes a 2.2-mile round-trip path to the pool below the cascade. Dukes Creek also belongs to the story of Georgia’s gold rush. Gold was found in the creek in 1828; discoveries in White County and neighboring Lumpkin County led to the rush. Beyond the falls, Dukes Creek flows into the Chattahoochee southeast of Helen, joining the river whose headwaters the byway encircles.
moments.notice: The falls drop on Davis Creek where it meets Dukes Creek.

moments.title: Hogpen Gap
moments.text: At Hogpen Gap, the byway crosses the Appalachian Trail, a meeting of the driving route and the footpath identified by the Forest Service.
